\chapter{More Short Replies}
\label{ch:sa-replies-more}
\hlchaptermodality{36}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say also, all, likewise, slowly and rightly in Sanskrit, and use any of the five on its own as a reply.}

Complete SA-C36-rightly and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[api]{\sk{अपि} (api) — also, too}

\label{lesson:SA-C36-also}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{śayyā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अपि}}
\textbf{\sk{अपि}} (\emph{api}) — \textquotedblleft{}also, too\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{अपि}} adds what you have just said to what came before. Put it after a word and you have piled that word on top: \emph{dugdham api}, \textquotedblleft{}milk as well\textquotedblright{}.

Greek \emph{epi-} is the same small word, and it fronts \emph{epidemic}, \emph{epilogue}, \emph{epicentre} and \emph{epitaph}. Latin \emph{ob} is a cousin too. It is short, it never changes shape, and it does a great deal of work.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A small word that adds one thing to another.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{api}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{śayyā}, then \emph{dugdham api}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{अपि} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}also, too\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sarvam]{\sk{सर्वम्} (sarvam) — all, the whole of it}

\label{lesson:SA-C36-all}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{api} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सर्वम्}}
\textbf{\sk{सर्वम्}} (\emph{sarvam}) — \textquotedblleft{}all, the whole of it\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{सर्वम्}} answers \textquotedblleft{}how much?\textquotedblright{} with \textquotedblleft{}all of it\textquotedblright{}, and it can stand alone as that answer.

Its cousins lean on \emph{whole} rather than on \emph{every}: Greek \emph{holos}, behind \emph{holistic} and \emph{catholic}; Latin \emph{sollus}, \textquotedblleft{}entire\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{salvus}, \textquotedblleft{}safe and whole\textquotedblright{}, behind \emph{save}, \emph{salvage} and \emph{salute}. \textbf{\sk{सर्वम्}}, \emph{holistic} and \emph{salvage} all start from one idea — nothing missing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A reply that says nothing has been left out.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sarvam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{api}, then \emph{sarvam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{सर्वम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}all, the whole of it\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tathā]{\sk{तथा} (tathā) — so, in that way, likewise}

\label{lesson:SA-C36-likewise}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{sarvam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तथा}}
\textbf{\sk{तथा}} (\emph{tathā}) — \textquotedblleft{}so, in that way, likewise\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{कथम्}}, which you have had for a long time, asks \textquotedblleft{}how?\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\sk{तथा}} answers it: \textquotedblleft{}that way\textquotedblright{}.

The \emph{t-} at the front is the one you met on \textbf{\sk{तत्}} and \textbf{\sk{तत्र}}, and it does the same job here — it points back at what has just been said. On its own, as a reply, \textbf{\sk{तथा}} means \textquotedblleft{}just so\textquotedblright{}, and doubled it agrees warmly: \emph{tathā tathā}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The answer that matches a question you have had since early on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tathā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{katham}, then \emph{tathā}, as question and answer
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{तथा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}so, in that way, likewise\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mandam]{\sk{मन्दम्} (mandam) — slowly, gently}

\label{lesson:SA-C36-slowly}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{tathā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मन्दम्}}
\textbf{\sk{मन्दम्}} (\emph{mandam}) — \textquotedblleft{}slowly, gently\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{मन्दम्}} asks for less speed. Doubled — \emph{mandam mandam} — it means \textquotedblleft{}slowly now, slowly\textquotedblright{}, which is how it is most often said.

This is the word you want when somebody is talking faster than you can follow, and it goes well with \textbf{\sk{कृपया}}: \emph{kṛpayā mandam}, \textquotedblleft{}slowly, please\textquotedblright{}. Said kindly, it repairs a conversation instead of stopping it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The repair word for a conversation moving too fast.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mandam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kṛpayā mandam}, said kindly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{मन्दम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}slowly, gently\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[samyak]{\sk{सम्यक्} (samyak) — rightly, properly, exactly so}

\label{lesson:SA-C36-rightly}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{mandam} mean, and what did \emph{api} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सम्यक्}}
\textbf{\sk{सम्यक्}} (\emph{samyak}) — \textquotedblleft{}rightly, properly, exactly so\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{सम्यक्}} confirms that a thing has been done right.

It is \emph{sam}, \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{sam-} inside \textbf{\sk{समुद्रः}} and \textbf{\sk{संस्कृतम्}} — joined to a piece meaning \textquotedblleft{}turned, directed\textquotedblright{}: turned the right way, all of a piece. Beside \textbf{\sk{साधु}} it is the cooler of the two. \textbf{\sk{साधु}} praises the person; \textbf{\sk{सम्यक्}} confirms the thing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five short replies, and the difference between praising and confirming.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{samyak}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{sādhu} and \emph{samyak} one after the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{सम्यक्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}rightly, properly, exactly so\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
